title: Carved lime-wood olive spoon
subtitle: Green-wood spoon-carving: a slotted serving spoon in lime
excerpt: A slotted olive spoon carved from a fresh lime billet. The slots drain the brine from olives or capers; the deep bowl holds a generous serving. Lime is the sculptor's standard for fine detail: soft and even-grained, forgiving under a sharp knife.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the slotted treen spoon method; Beeton's Book of Household Management (1861) for olive serving pieces and dimensions.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Soft and easy to carve under hand tools.

content.text: A slotted olive spoon has two or three drainage slots cut through the bowl to drain brine from olives or capers as you serve them. Lime wood is the carver's first choice for fine work: soft and even-grained, with a pale surface where detail cuts read clearly. The project is intermediate because the drainage slots need a stop cut before the bowl hollow is carved, and the slot walls need careful refining after sawing.
. Lime from a managed coppice or a lime-avenue pruning is ideal.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one, the dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.

One lime billet roughly 28 cm long and 6 cm across, split to give a flat face. Lime (Tilia europaea) is food-safe once finished with a drying oil and is the traditional carving lime (basswood in North America). The pale cream colour stays consistent as the spoon ages under linseed oil. Sycamore is a direct substitute, slightly harder, equally food-safe, equally even-grained.
Sloyd knife for shaping handle and outside of bowl.
Hook knife, medium, for the bowl hollow.
Coping saw for cutting the drainage slots.
Detail knife for refining the slot edges.
A low stool with a folded leather apron across the lap. Good side lighting to see the slot edges clearly.

Split the billet along the pith. Draw the spoon profile on the flat face: bowl 7 cm long and 5 cm wide, handle 20 cm. Mark three parallel slots across the widest part of the bowl, each 3 cm long and 5 mm wide, running roughly perpendicular to the handle axis.

around all four sides of each slot location, cutting straight down through the blank thickness to define the slot boundary. Then use the coping saw to remove the waste inside each slot, working carefully within the stop-cut lines. The stop cuts prevent the coping saw blade from tearing the grain beyond the slot edge. Clean the slot walls with the detail knife using push cuts down each wall face.

Turn the blank over. Use push cuts to carve a shallow dome on the back of the bowl, deeper than a jam spoon back, about 8 mm below the shoulder at the centre. Work evenly either side of each slot so the bowl walls around the slots are the same thickness.

Step 6: Refine the handle and final surface
to taper the handle and refine the transition between bowl and handle. A final pass with 240-grit sandpaper inside the slot walls if needed, then leave to dry.

Let the spoon dry for three days before oiling. Apply raw linseed oil all over including through the slots. Soak for one hour, wipe off the surplus, repeat after twenty-four hours. Cure for two weeks before food contact.
Two slots only: a simpler version with just two slots is easier to clean and good for capers.
Longer handle: 25 cm handle works better for serving from a deep jar.
Hand wash only. Dry immediately after washing. Re-oil when the wood looks pale. The slots need particular attention when oiling, apply with a small cloth or cotton bud to get into the slot corners.

attrs.symptom: The grain tears at the slot edge during coping-saw cutting
attrs.cause: No stop cut was made before sawing
attrs.fix: Always make the stop-cut boundary before using the saw. The stop cut severs the grain at the intended edge; without it the saw vibration tears the grain past the line.

attrs.symptom: The bowl walls between slots are too thin and flex
attrs.cause: Hook knife hollowed too deeply between the slots
attrs.fix: Keep a minimum of 4 mm wall thickness between adjacent slots. If the wall has already gone thin, sand it smooth and accept the thinner wall; do not try to add wood back.
